```rust
            // No selection yet: forward starts at the first candidate, backward at the last, so the
            // first press of either key selects something instead of appearing to do nothing.
            (None, false) => 0,
            (None, true) => candidates.len() - 1,
        };
        self.selection = Some(candidates[next]);
    }

    /// Advance the held-key repeat by `dt` and fire each held camera action the right number of times.
    ///
    /// The accumulator is the whole point: a 144 fps frame fires zero or one repeat rather than 7.2, so
    /// the camera travels the same distance per second on every machine. The clamped `dt` is the second
    /// half — a frame that took four seconds (a stall, a breakpoint, a window drag) must not teleport
    /// the camera across the ward, and clamping the *elapsed time* is how that is prevented without
    /// dropping the input entirely.
    /// The floating panel the surface will actually draw, or `None` if none is open.
    ///
    /// **Exclusive, and by geometry rather than taste.** The keymap wants 900×560 and the proposals
    /// panel 760×520; inside a 1400-point window's canvas column those two cannot both fit, so a
    /// surface that drew every open panel would draw them on top of each other — the defect
    /// `regions.rs` exists to report. One at a time is what the sizes permit.
    ///
    /// The rule lives **here rather than in the toggle handlers**, on purpose: a bit that is set but
    /// not drawn is a state the surface has to be able to describe, and an invariant enforced in the
    /// handlers is invisible to a test that sets the bits directly. See [`Self::hidden_floats`].
    pub fn topmost_float(&self) -> Option<crate::regions::FloatKind> {
        use crate::regions::FloatKind;
        [
            (FloatKind::Help, self.show_help),
            (FloatKind::Ledger, self.show_ledger),
            (FloatKind::Proposals, self.show_proposals),
            (FloatKind::Debug, self.show_debug),
        ]
        .iter()
        .filter(|(_, open)| *open)
        .map(|(kind, _)| *kind)
        .min_by_key(|kind| kind.rank())
    }

    /// How many open panels are **not** drawn, because the surface shows one at a time.
    ///
    /// Reported rather than dropped. A panel that vanished without a word is indistinguishable from a
    /// binding that does not work, and this surface's whole discipline is that a limit is stated
    /// rather than implied.
    pub fn hidden_floats(&self) -> usize {
        let open = [
            self.show_help,
            self.show_ledger,
            self.show_proposals,
            self.show_debug,
        ]
        .iter()
        .filter(|open| **open)
        .count();
        open.saturating_sub(usize::from(self.topmost_float().is_some()))
    }

    pub fn tick_held(&mut self, held: &[Action], dt: f32, extent: f32, grid: (f32, f32, i32)) {
        // A stalled frame (window drag, breakpoint, a slow rebuild) must not fling the camera across
        // the ward, so the elapsed time is CLAMPED before it enters the clock. Clamping the time and
        // not the repeats is the point: the owed count is then derived from a bounded clock, so it is
        // bounded too, and the hard cap below is a second line rather than the only one.
        self.held_clock += dt.clamp(0.0, 0.25) as f64;
        let owed = (self.held_clock * KEY_REPEAT_HZ as f64) as u64;
        let mut remaining = owed.saturating_sub(self.held_spent).min(32);
        self.held_spent = owed;
        while remaining > 0 {
            remaining -= 1;
            for action in held.iter().filter(|a| a.is_camera()).copied() {
                self.apply(action, extent, grid);
            }
        }
    }

    /// How many repeats the held keys have spent. Telemetry for the debug HUD, and the value the
    /// frame-rate-independence test reads so it does not have to infer the count from camera math.
    pub fn held_repeats(&self) -> u64 {
        self.held_spent
    }

    /// Which action a key maps to **given the modifier state**.
    ///
    /// The modifier is part of the lookup rather than a separate table because `Shift+arrow` and `arrow`
    /// resolve to different actions on the same key, and a matcher that ignored the modifier would make
    /// the brush unreachable by keyboard while still passing "the key is bound" tests. Returns the first
    /// match in table order, so a duplicate binding is resolved deterministically rather than by
    /// iteration order — and a test asserts no duplicate exists at all.
    pub fn action_for(key: egui::Key, modifiers: &egui::Modifiers) -> Option<Action> {
        let plain = KEYMAP
            .iter()
            .find(|(k, m, ..)| *k == key && *m == Mod::None);
        let shifted = KEYMAP
            .iter()
            .find(|(k, m, ..)| *k == key && *m == Mod::Shift);
        match (shifted, plain) {
            // A key with a Shift binding uses only that binding while Shift is held: the modifier
            // selects, it does not fall through. Falling through would make Shift+arrow pan AND grow.
            (Some((_, _, action, ..)), _) if modifiers.shift => Some(*action),
            (_, Some((_, _, action, ..))) if !modifiers.shift => Some(*action),
            _ => None,
        }
    }

    /// Every binding whose action matches, as `(chord, group, description)`. The panel uses this to
    /// print the shortcut beside each palette entry, so a button and its key cannot disagree.
    pub fn chords_for(action: Action) -> Vec<(&'static str, &'static str)> {
        KEYMAP
            .iter()
            .filter(|(_, _, a, ..)| *a == action)
            .map(|(key, m, _, _, desc)| (chord(*key, *m), *desc))
            .collect()
    }

    /// The keymap grouped for the help overlay. Generated from `KEYMAP`, so it cannot document a
    /// binding that does not exist.
    pub fn help_groups() -> Vec<(&'static str, Vec<(&'static str, &'static str)>)> {
        let mut groups: Vec<(&'static str, Vec<(&'static str, &'static str)>)> = Vec::new();
        for (key, m, _, group, desc) in KEYMAP {
            let name = chord(*key, *m);
            match groups.iter_mut().find(|(g, _)| g == group) {
                Some((_, rows)) => rows.push((name, desc)),
                None => groups.push((group, vec![(name, desc)])),
            }
        }
        groups
    }
}

/// A rendered chord: `Shift+↑`, `Space`, `+`.
///
/// `'static` strings rather than a `String`, because the only parts are a table constant and a `'static`
/// modifier prefix — allocating per row per frame to render a keymap would be the surface spending its
/// budget on nothing.
pub fn chord(key: egui::Key, modifier: Mod) -> &'static str {
    match (modifier, key) {
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::ArrowUp) => "Shift+↑",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::ArrowDown) => "Shift+↓",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::ArrowLeft) => "Shift+←",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::ArrowRight) => "Shift+→",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::Num1) => "Shift+1",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::Num2) => "Shift+2",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::Num3) => "Shift+3",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::Num4) => "Shift+4",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::Num5) => "Shift+5",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::Num6) => "Shift+6",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::W) => "Shift+W",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::A) => "Shift+A",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::S) => "Shift+S",
        (Mod::Shift, egui::Key::D) => "Shift+D",
        (Mod::Shift, _) => "Shift+·",
        (Mod::None, k) => key_name(k),
    }
}

pub fn key_name(key: egui::Key) -> &'static str {
    match key {
        egui::Key::ArrowUp => "↑",
        egui::Key::ArrowDown => "↓",
        egui::Key::ArrowLeft => "←",
        egui::Key::ArrowRight => "→",
        egui::Key::Escape => "Esc",
        egui::Key::Enter => "Enter",
        egui::Key::Space => "Space",
        egui::Key::Tab => "Tab",
        egui::Key::Home => "Home",
        egui::Key::Plus | egui::Key::Equals => "+",
        egui::Key::Minus => "−",
        egui::Key::PageUp => "PgUp",
        egui::Key::PageDown => "PgDn",
        egui::Key::Num0 => "0",
        egui::Key::Num1 => "1",
        egui::Key::Num2 => "2",
        egui::Key::Num3 => "3",
        egui::Key::Num4 => "4",
        egui::Key::Num5 => "5",
        egui::Key::Num6 => "6",
        egui::Key::Num7 => "7",
        egui::Key::Num8 => "8",
        egui::Key::Num9 => "9",
        egui::Key::F1 => "F1",
        egui::Key::F => "F",
        egui::Key::G => "G",
        egui::Key::V => "V",
        egui::Key::M => "M",
        egui::Key::L => "L",
        egui::Key::P => "P",
        egui::Key::Q => "Q",
        egui::Key::R => "R",
        egui::Key::T => "T",
        egui::Key::W => "W",
        egui::Key::A => "A",
        egui::Key::S => "S",
        egui::Key::D => "D",
        egui::Key::E => "E",
        egui::Key::Backtick => "`",
        egui::Key::Slash | egui::Key::Questionmark => "?",
        egui::Key::X => "X",
        egui::Key::Backspace => "⌫",
        egui::Key::OpenBracket => "[",
        egui::Key::CloseBracket => "]",
        egui::Key::Delete => "Del",
        _ => "·",
    }
}

/// The HIG audit `3DUI.MD` §17 asks for: each rule, whether it is implemented, and **what was
/// actually done** rather than a bare boolean. A rule reported as implemented with no statement of
/// how is a rule nobody can check.
pub fn hig_audit() -> Vec<(&'static str, bool, &'static str)> {
    vec![
        ("SL-01 centre FOV", true, "focus point is always the projection centre"),
        (
            "SL-02 1–2m depth",
            true,
            "honoured as a RATIO: depth is a clamped multiple of the grid extent, because the world is 24 tiles and not a room",
        ),
        (
            "SL-03 no behind-user",
            true,
            "yaw clamped to ±120° and pitch to 12–78°, so the camera cannot pass the horizon or the horizon-pole",
        ),
        ("SL-04 personal space", true, "near plane fixed at 0.5 world units"),
        ("SL-05 Z-depth", true, "HUD panels drawn over the scene, never inside it"),
        ("SL-06 120° arc", true, "decision monuments placed on a 120° arc, not a ring"),
        (
            "SL-07 environment anchors",
            true,
            "labels are projected from world space and fade with distance",
        ),
    ]
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    fn extent() -> f32 {
        crate::gpu::scene::grid_extent(24)
    }

    #[test]
    fn no_action_can_put_the_camera_under_the_ground() {
        // The failure this prevents is not a crash, it is a camera below y=0 that renders the
        // underside of every tile and reads as a rendering bug rather than a missing clamp.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        for _ in 0..200 {
            c.apply(Action::PitchDown, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.pitch() >= Limits::PITCH_MIN - 1e-6);
        assert!(c.orbit.eye(extent())[1] > 0.0, "the eye must stay above the ground");
        for _ in 0..400 {
            c.apply(Action::PitchUp, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.pitch() <= Limits::PITCH_MAX + 1e-6);
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_camera_cannot_leave_the_forward_hemisphere() {
        // SL-03. Yaw is clamped on BOTH sides, and the clamp survives repeated input — the property
        // that matters, since a single-shot clamp is trivially true and useless.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        for _ in 0..500 {
            c.apply(Action::OrbitRight, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.yaw() <= Limits::YAW_MAX + 1e-6, "yaw {}", c.orbit.yaw());
        for _ in 0..1000 {
            c.apply(Action::OrbitLeft, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.yaw() >= Limits::YAW_MIN - 1e-6, "yaw {}", c.orbit.yaw());
    }

    #[test]
    fn zoom_is_logarithmic_and_bounded() {
        // A linear zoom feels fast when close and useless when far. The test asserts both the bound
        // and the log property: equal scroll deltas produce equal RATIOS.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        let a = c.orbit.zoom;
        c.apply(Action::ZoomIn, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        let b = c.orbit.zoom;
        c.apply(Action::ZoomIn, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        let d = c.orbit.zoom;
        assert!((b / a - d / b).abs() < 1e-4, "zoom is not multiplicative: {a} {b} {d}");
        for _ in 0..200 {
            c.apply(Action::ZoomOut, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.zoom >= Limits::ZOOM_MIN - 1e-6);
        for _ in 0..400 {
            c.apply(Action::ZoomIn, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.zoom <= Limits::ZOOM_MAX + 1e-6);
    }

    #[test]
    fn panning_cannot_lose_the_city() {
        // A camera that can wander to infinity on a finite grid is one whose user cannot get back.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        let e = extent();
        for _ in 0..2000 {
            c.apply(Action::PanEast, e, (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.focus[0].abs() <= e * 1.4, "focus x = {}", c.orbit.focus[0]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn reset_returns_the_views_own_camera() {
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.apply(Action::OrbitRight, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        c.apply(Action::ZoomIn, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        c.apply(Action::ResetCamera, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert!((c.orbit.pitch() - 30.0_f32.to_radians()).abs() < 1e-5);
        assert!((c.orbit.yaw() - 45.0_f32.to_radians()).abs() < 1e-5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn escape_cancels_a_drag_and_clears_the_tool() {
        // A drag the user has decided against must have a way out that is not "finish it anyway".
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.tool = Tool::Zone(2);
        c.drag = Drag::Zone { from: [1, 1], to: [4, 4] };
        c.apply(Action::Cancel, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert_eq!(c.drag, Drag::None, "Escape must abort a drag in progress");
        assert_eq!(c.tool, Tool::Select, "Escape must clear the active tool");

        // And the same through the keymap, so the binding and the behaviour cannot diverge.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.tool = Tool::Zone(1);
        c.drag = Drag::Orbit;
        c.apply(press(egui::Key::Escape), extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert_eq!(c.drag, Drag::None);
        assert_eq!(c.tool, Tool::Select);
    }

    #[test]
    fn every_action_the_state_machine_defines_is_reachable() {
        // A variant nothing can construct is a control that reads as implemented and has no way in —
        // §6.4's decoration-provenance defect applied to this module. The concrete case that prompted
        // this test: `Action::Cancel` existed, was matched in `apply`, and the keymap bound Escape to
        // `SelectTool` instead, so the whole escalating-dismiss path was unreachable from the keyboard.
        //
        // The allow-list is named rather than implied, so a *new* unreachable variant fails this test
        // instead of being absorbed into a growing silent set.
        const UI_ONLY: &[Action] = &[Action::SelectTool];
        for action in ALL_ACTIONS {
            if UI_ONLY.contains(action) {
                continue;
            }
            let bound = KEYMAP.iter().any(|(_, _, a, ..)| a == action);
            assert!(
                bound,
                "{action:?} is bound to no key and is not in the UI_ONLY allow-list; \
                 either bind it or say why it is unreachable"
            );
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_node_palette_is_reachable_by_digit_all_the_way_to_the_end() {
        // `NODE_KINDS` has six entries; only `7`/`8`/`9` were bound, so three of the six nodes had no
        // fast route. The zone palette got `1`–`6` and the node palette got three digits, which is the
        // kind of asymmetry that is invisible until someone counts.
        for index in 0..6 {
            let bound = KEYMAP
                .iter()
                .any(|(_, _, a, ..)| *a == Action::NodeTool(index));
            assert!(bound, "node kind {index} has no digit binding");
        }
        for index in 0..6 {
            let bound = KEYMAP.iter().any(|(_, _, a, ..)| *a == Action::ZoneTool(index));
            assert!(bound, "zone kind {index} has no digit binding");
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_depth_band_has_a_binding_and_stays_inside_it() {
        // SL-02. `Orbit::depth_by` was clamped, tested and **called by nothing** — the rule was reported
        // honoured by `hig_audit` while having no control at all. This asserts the binding exists AND
        // that driving it hard cannot leave the band.
        assert!(KEYMAP.iter().any(|(_, _, a, ..)| *a == Action::DepthIn));
        assert!(KEYMAP.iter().any(|(_, _, a, ..)| *a == Action::DepthOut));
        assert!(Action::DepthIn.is_camera(), "depth must repeat while held");

        let mut c = Controls::default();
        for _ in 0..500 {
            c.apply(Action::DepthIn, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.depth() >= Limits::DEPTH_MIN - 1e-6, "{}", c.orbit.depth());
        for _ in 0..500 {
            c.apply(Action::DepthOut, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert!(c.orbit.depth() <= Limits::DEPTH_MAX + 1e-6, "{}", c.orbit.depth());
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_cursor_describes_the_gesture_that_is_actually_in_flight() {
        // The cursor is derived, so it cannot lag the state. Each assertion is a statement about what
        // the next press would do, read off the same struct the press handler reads.
        let mut c = Controls::default();

        // Over chrome: nothing to act on.
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(true), Cursor::Default);
        // Off the ward: the tool does not advertise itself.
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(false), Cursor::Default);

        c.hover = Some([4, 4]);
        // Select over a tile: a press picks it.
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(false), Cursor::PointingHand);
        // A zone tool over a tile: a press draws.
        c.tool = Tool::Zone(0);
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(false), Cursor::Crosshair);
        // Chrome outranks the tool, because the press would land on a panel.
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(true), Cursor::Default);

        // A gesture in flight outranks the tool that started it.
        c.drag = Drag::Orbit;
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(false), Cursor::Grabbing);
        c.drag = Drag::Pan;
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(false), Cursor::Grabbing);
        c.drag = Drag::Zone { from: [1, 1], to: [3, 3] };
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(false), Cursor::Crosshair);

        // The failure this catches: a drag ends and the cursor is left describing the gesture.
        c.drag = Drag::None;
        c.tool = Tool::Select;
        assert_eq!(c.cursor(false), Cursor::PointingHand);
    }

    #[test]
    fn escape_escalates_from_the_tool_down_to_nothing() {
        // The escalating dismiss, and the invariant that makes it usable: Escape always makes progress
        // and never leaves the surface in a state it was already in. The pre-fix behaviour was that
        // Escape cleared the tool but left the brush, so the rectangle survived the key that was
        // supposed to abandon it and the next Enter committed it anyway.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.tool = Tool::Zone(3);
        c.brush = Some(([2, 2], [6, 6]));
        c.drag = Drag::Zone { from: [2, 2], to: [6, 6] };

        c.apply(Action::Cancel, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert_eq!(c.drag, Drag::None, "Escape must abort the drag");
        assert_eq!(c.brush, None, "Escape must abandon the rectangle, not just the tool");
        assert_eq!(c.tool, Tool::Select, "Escape must clear the tool");
        assert!(c.brush_tiles().is_empty(), "an abandoned brush must cover no tiles");

        // Idempotent: pressing it again is a no-op rather than a state the surface cannot leave.
        c.apply(Action::Cancel, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert_eq!(c.tool, Tool::Select);
        assert_eq!(c.brush, None);
    }

    fn press(key: egui::Key) -> Action {
        Controls::action_for(key, &egui::Modifiers::NONE).expect("the key must be bound")
    }

    fn press_shift(key: egui::Key) -> Action {
        Controls::action_for(key, &egui::Modifiers::SHIFT).expect("the shifted key must be bound")
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_keymap_has_no_duplicate_chord() {
        // A duplicated CHORD — the key together with its modifier — means one action is unreachable and
        // the help lists a binding that does not fire, and both failures are invisible without this
        // check. The key alone is not the unit: `↑` and `Shift+↑` are two different chords and must both
        // be allowed, which is why this asserts on the pair rather than on the key.
        let mut seen: Vec<(egui::Key, Mod)> = Vec::new();
        for (key, modifier, ..) in KEYMAP {
            assert!(
                !seen.contains(&(*key, *modifier)),
                "{key:?} with {modifier:?} is bound twice"
            );
            seen.push((*key, *modifier));
        }
        // The shipped table really does use both modifiers on one key — otherwise this test would be
        // asserting a distinction nothing exercises.
        assert!(seen.contains(&(egui::Key::ArrowUp, Mod::None)));
        assert!(seen.contains(&(egui::Key::ArrowUp, Mod::Shift)));
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_help_overlay_renders_a_modified_chord_differently_from_a_plain_one() {
        // If both rendered as "↑" the help would list the same key twice with two descriptions, which
        // reads as a documentation bug and hides the fact that the brush exists.
        assert_eq!(chord(egui::Key::ArrowUp, Mod::None), "↑");
        assert_eq!(chord(egui::Key::ArrowUp, Mod::Shift), "Shift+↑");
        let rows: Vec<&str> = Controls::help_groups()
            .into_iter()
            .flat_map(|(_, rows)| rows.into_iter().map(|(k, _)| k))
            .collect();
        assert!(rows.contains(&"Shift+↑"), "the brush quartet must appear in the help");
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_help_overlay_cannot_document_a_binding_that_does_not_exist() {
        // Generated from KEYMAP, so the two cannot drift.
        let groups = Controls::help_groups();
        let rows: usize = groups.iter().map(|(_, r)| r.len()).sum();
        assert_eq!(rows, KEYMAP.len());
        assert!(groups.iter().any(|(g, _)| *g == "Camera"));
        assert!(groups.iter().any(|(g, _)| *g == "Overlays"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_specs_ledger_key_is_documented_as_deviating() {
        // §3.3 says `D`; D is pan-east. The deviation must be visible in the table rather than a
        // silent difference between the spec and the app.
        assert_eq!(Controls::action_for(egui::Key::D, &egui::Modifiers::NONE), Some(Action::PanEast));
        assert_eq!(Controls::action_for(egui::Key::L, &egui::Modifiers::NONE), Some(Action::ToggleLedger));
        assert_eq!(Controls::action_for(egui::Key::P, &egui::Modifiers::NONE), Some(Action::ToggleProposals));
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // The brush — the keyboard path for the drag gesture (HIG)
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    #[test]
    fn shift_arrow_and_plain_arrow_are_different_actions() {
        // The defect this prevents is precise and was the first thing the modifier split fixed: with a
        // matcher that ignored modifiers, `Shift+↑` panned the camera and the brush had NO keyboard path
        // while every "the key is bound" test still passed.
        assert_eq!(press(egui::Key::ArrowUp), Action::PanNorth);
        assert_eq!(press_shift(egui::Key::ArrowUp), Action::BrushNorth);
        assert_eq!(press_shift(egui::Key::ArrowRight), Action::BrushEast);
        assert_ne!(press(egui::Key::ArrowUp), press_shift(egui::Key::ArrowUp));
        // And no action is reachable with the wrong modifier, so the table cannot be read loosely.
        assert_eq!(Controls::action_for(egui::Key::X, &egui::Modifiers::SHIFT), None);
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_brush_grows_from_the_selection_and_stays_on_the_grid() {
        let grid = (30.0, 45.0, 24);
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.selection = Some([10, 10]);
        c.apply(Action::BrushEast, extent(), grid);
        c.apply(Action::BrushEast, extent(), grid);
        c.apply(Action::BrushSouth, extent(), grid);
        assert_eq!(c.brush, Some(([10, 10], [12, 11])));
        assert_eq!(c.brush_tiles().len(), 3 * 2);

        // Off the grid: the corner stops at the edge rather than wrapping or panicking.
        let mut far = Controls::default();
        far.selection = Some([23, 23]);
        for _ in 0..40 {
            far.apply(Action::BrushEast, extent(), grid);
            far.apply(Action::BrushSouth, extent(), grid);
        }
        assert_eq!(far.brush, Some(([23, 23], [23, 23])), "the brush left the ward");
    }

    #[test]
    fn each_shrink_key_is_the_exact_inverse_of_its_grow_key() {
        // An "undo" that is not the inverse of the action it undoes is worse than no undo: the player
        // presses it, the rectangle changes in a direction they did not predict, and there is no way to
        // reason about the state. Asserted for all four axes rather than for one.
        let grid = (30.0, 45.0, 24);
        let pairs = [
            (Action::BrushNorth, Action::ShrinkNorth),
            (Action::BrushSouth, Action::ShrinkSouth),
            (Action::BrushWest, Action::ShrinkWest),
            (Action::BrushEast, Action::ShrinkEast),
        ];
        for (grow, shrink) in pairs {
            let mut c = Controls::default();
            c.selection = Some([12, 12]);
            for _ in 0..3 {
                c.apply(grow, extent(), grid);
            }
            let grown = c.brush;
            assert_ne!(grown, Some(([12, 12], [12, 12])), "{grow:?} did not grow");
            c.apply(shrink, extent(), grid);
            assert_ne!(c.brush, grown, "{shrink:?} did not shrink");
            c.apply(grow, extent(), grid);
            assert_eq!(c.brush, grown, "{shrink:?} is not the inverse of {grow:?}");
        }

        // Shrinking to and past the anchor saturates on a 1-tile rectangle rather than inverting.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.selection = Some([12, 12]);
        for _ in 0..5 {
            c.apply(Action::ShrinkEast, extent(), grid);
        }
        let (from, to) = c.brush.expect("a brush exists once a brush key is pressed");
        assert_eq!(from, to, "the brush inverted instead of collapsing to its anchor");
    }

    #[test]
    fn escape_also_discards_the_brush() {
        // A rectangle the user has decided against must have a way out that is not "commit it anyway".
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.selection = Some([4, 4]);
        c.apply(Action::BrushEast, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert!(c.brush.is_some());
        c.apply(Action::ClearBrush, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert!(c.brush.is_none(), "X must discard the brush");
        c.apply(Action::BrushEast, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        c.apply(Action::SelectTool, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert!(c.brush.is_none(), "Escape must discard the brush");
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_tool_cycle_wraps_in_both_directions() {
        // `[`/`]` is the discoverable path to a tool; the numerals stay as accelerators. A cycle that
        // does not wrap makes the last tool unreachable going forward, which is a tool the player
        // cannot select from the position they are most likely to be in.
        let grid = (30.0, 45.0, 24);
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.tool = Tool::Zone(0);
        c.apply(Action::PickToolPrev, extent(), grid);
        assert_eq!(c.tool, Tool::Zone(ZONE_KINDS.len() - 1), "backwards must wrap to the end");
        c.apply(Action::PickToolNext, extent(), grid);
        assert_eq!(c.tool, Tool::Zone(0), "forwards must wrap to the start");
        // and a node tool stays in the node palette rather than jumping to a zone
        c.tool = Tool::Node(0);
        c.apply(Action::PickToolNext, extent(), grid);
        assert_eq!(c.tool, Tool::Node(1));
    }

    #[test]
    fn tab_cycles_the_selection_and_saturates_on_an_empty_view() {
        let candidates = [[1, 1], [5, 5], [9, 9]];
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.cycle_selection(&candidates, false);
        assert_eq!(c.selection, Some([1, 1]), "the first press must select something");
        c.cycle_selection(&candidates, false);
        assert_eq!(c.selection, Some([5, 5]));
        c.cycle_selection(&candidates, true);
        assert_eq!(c.selection, Some([1, 1]));
        // Backward from no selection starts at the last, so neither direction is a no-op.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.cycle_selection(&candidates, true);
        assert_eq!(c.selection, Some([9, 9]));
        // A view with no loci clears the selection rather than leaving a highlight over nothing.
        c.cycle_selection(&[], false);
        assert_eq!(c.selection, None);
    }

    #[test]
    fn middle_drag_is_a_pan_gesture_and_is_its_own_drag_state() {
        // The gap this closes: panning was keyboard-only, so a mouse user could orbit and zoom but not
        // travel. Three drag states rather than a bool, so two gestures cannot interleave silently.
        assert_ne!(Drag::Pan, Drag::Orbit);
        assert_ne!(Drag::Pan, Drag::None);
        let mut o = Orbit::default();
        o.pan_by(3.0, -2.0, extent());
        assert!((o.focus[0] - 3.0).abs() < 1e-6);
        assert!((o.focus[1] + 2.0).abs() < 1e-6);
    }

    #[test]
    fn every_palette_action_has_at_least_one_chord_to_print() {
        // The palette prints the shortcut beside each entry. An action with no chord must print nothing
        // rather than an invented key, and every action that IS bound must be findable here — otherwise
        // a button would advertise a key that does nothing.
        for i in 0..ZONE_KINDS.len() {
            assert!(
                !Controls::chords_for(Action::ZoneTool(i)).is_empty(),
                "zone tool {i} is bound in the table but has no chord"
            );
        }
        assert!(Controls::chords_for(Action::ToggleHelp).len() >= 2, "`?` and F1 both open help");
        assert!(!Controls::chords_for(Action::ClearBrush).is_empty());
        // The chords are rendered, not blank: a palette showing "" beside a button is a lie by omission.
        for (chord, _) in Controls::chords_for(Action::PanEast) {
            assert!(!chord.is_empty() && chord != "·", "pan-east rendered as {chord:?}");
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn every_hig_rule_is_reported_with_a_statement_not_just_a_tick() {
        let audit = hig_audit();
        assert_eq!(audit.len(), 7, "SL-01 through SL-07");
        for (rule, implemented, how) in audit {
            assert!(implemented, "{rule} is not implemented");
            assert!(how.len() > 20, "{rule} reports no statement of how it was done");
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_zone_tools_are_the_six_the_palette_draws() {
        for i in 0..ZONE_KINDS.len() {
            let t = Tool::Zone(i);
            assert_eq!(t.zone_index(), Some(i));
            assert_eq!(t.label(), ZONE_KINDS[i]);
        }
        for i in 0..NODE_KINDS.len() {
            assert_eq!(Tool::Node(i).node_index(), Some(i));
        }
        // Out of range is not a panic: a tool index from a stale save must degrade, not crash.
        assert_eq!(Tool::Zone(99).label(), "zone");
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_projection_is_orthographic_so_scale_is_uniform() {
        // The property that makes an isometric city readable: two identical citizens are the same
        // size wherever they stand. A perspective projection would break it, so it is asserted rather
        // than left to a comment.
        let o = Orbit::default();
        let m = o.view_proj(1.6, extent());
        // The no-perspective condition is that the CLIP W is the view W, i.e. row 3 of the matrix is
        // `(0, 0, 0, 1)`: no input coordinate can influence the divisor, so no point shrinks with
        // distance. The first draft asserted `m[3][2] == 0`, which is the projection's *translation*
        // term and is `-near * nf` for a perfectly orthographic matrix — it failed because the
        // assertion was about the wrong element, not because the projection had become perspective.
        assert!((m[3][3] - 1.0).abs() < 1e-6);
        assert_eq!(m[0][3], 0.0, "clip x must not contribute to clip w");
        assert_eq!(m[1][3], 0.0, "clip y must not contribute to clip w");
        assert_eq!(m[2][3], 0.0, "clip z must not contribute to clip w");

        // The property in the title, asserted directly: **a fixed world delta produces a fixed screen
        // delta wherever it is**. That is what "uniform scale" means, and it is the thing a perspective
        // projection breaks. The first draft instead compared `m[0][0]` against `1 / half_width`, which
        // is only the answer for an unrotated camera — with a 45° yaw the composite column is scaled by
        // `right.x`, so the assertion failed on a correct matrix.
        let project = |p: [f32; 3]| {
            let w = [
                m[0][0] * p[0] + m[1][0] * p[1] + m[2][0] * p[2] + m[3][0],
                m[0][1] * p[0] + m[1][1] * p[1] + m[2][1] * p[2] + m[3][1],
            ];
            w
        };
        let delta = [1.0f32, 0.0, 0.0];
        let near_pair = (project([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), project(delta));
        let far_pair = (project([3.0, 0.0, -4.0]), project([4.0, 0.0, -4.0]));
        for axis in 0..2 {
            let d_near = near_pair.1[axis] - near_pair.0[axis];
            let d_far = far_pair.1[axis] - far_pair.0[axis];
            assert!(
                (d_near - d_far).abs() < 1e-6,
                "the same world delta projected to {d_near} near and {d_far} far — scale is not uniform"
            );
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_view_matrix_puts_the_target_at_the_origin_of_view_space() {
        let o = Orbit::default();
        let e = extent();
        let v = look_at(o.eye(e), o.target(), [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]);
        // Transform the target through the view matrix; it must land on (0,0,-distance).
        let t = o.target();
        let x = v[0][0] * t[0] + v[1][0] * t[1] + v[2][0] * t[2] + v[3][0];
        let y = v[0][1] * t[0] + v[1][1] * t[1] + v[2][1] * t[2] + v[3][1];
        assert!(x.abs() < 1e-3, "target x in view space = {x}");
        assert!(y.abs() < 1e-3, "target y in view space = {y}");
    }

    #[test]
    fn depth_maps_the_near_plane_to_zero_and_the_far_plane_to_one() {
        // wgpu's depth convention. Getting this wrong produces geometry that clips for no visible
        // reason, and the bug looks like a culling problem.
        let m = ortho(10.0, 10.0, 2.0, 50.0);
        let z_clip = |z_eye: f32| m[2][2] * z_eye + m[3][2];
        // eye-space z is negative in front of the camera
        assert!(z_clip(-2.0).abs() < 1e-5, "near plane -> {}", z_clip(-2.0));
        assert!((z_clip(-50.0) - 1.0).abs() < 1e-5, "far plane -> {}", z_clip(-50.0));
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Picking — the inverse of the projection, which is the only way a click can be trusted
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    /// Project a world point to normalised view-rect coordinates, the inverse of `ground_at`.
    fn project(o: &Orbit, world: [f32; 3], aspect: f32, extent: f32) -> [f32; 2] {
        let m = o.view_proj(aspect, extent);
        let clip = [
            m[0][0] * world[0] + m[1][0] * world[1] + m[2][0] * world[2] + m[3][0],
            m[0][1] * world[0] + m[1][1] * world[1] + m[2][1] * world[2] + m[3][1],
            m[0][3] * world[0] + m[1][3] * world[1] + m[2][3] * world[2] + m[3][3],
        ];
        let ndc = [clip[0] / clip[2], clip[1] / clip[2]];
        [(ndc[0] + 1.0) * 0.5, (1.0 - ndc[1]) * 0.5]
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_click_lands_on_the_tile_the_renderer_drew_there() {
        // The round trip that makes the surface usable: project a tile centre, then pick it back out.
        // Without this, a click could land one tile away from the citizen under the cursor and nothing
        // in the build would say so — the projection and the picking would each be ``correct''.
        let aspect = 1.6;
        let size = 24;
        let e = crate::gpu::scene::grid_extent(size);
        for (tilt, rotation, zoom) in [(30.0, 45.0, 28.0), (12.0, -60.0, 12.0), (70.0, 100.0, 60.0)] {
            let mut o = Orbit::from_grid(tilt, rotation, size);
            o.zoom = zoom;
            for tile in [[0, 0], [1, 23], [12, 12], [23, 0], [7, 18]] {
                let world = crate::gpu::scene::tile_world(tile, size);
                let uv = project(&o, world, aspect, e);
                let picked = o.tile_at(uv, aspect, e, size).unwrap_or_else(|| {
                    panic!("tile {tile:?} at tilt {tilt} rotation {rotation} zoom {zoom} picked nothing (uv {uv:?})")
                });
                assert_eq!(picked, tile, "tilt {tilt} rotation {rotation} zoom {zoom}");
            }
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_pointer_outside_the_ward_picks_nothing_rather_than_an_edge_tile() {
        // Clamping would turn "outside the grid" into "on the last tile", and the player would be
        // proposing zones on tiles they never pointed at.
        let o = Orbit::default();
        let e = crate::gpu::scene::grid_extent(24);
        assert!(o.tile_at([-0.4, 0.5], 1.6, e, 24).is_none());
        assert!(o.tile_at([0.5, -0.4], 1.6, e, 24).is_none());
        assert!(o.tile_at([1.4, 0.5], 1.6, e, 24).is_none());
        assert!(o.tile_at([0.5, 0.5], 1.6, e, 24).is_some());
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_camera_cannot_be_driven_to_the_horizon_at_all() {
        // `ground_at` returns `None` when `forward.y` is ~0, and that guard is **unreachable through
        // the public API** — `PITCH_MIN` stops the camera at 12 degrees. Both are kept: the clamp is
        // what a user experiences, and the guard is what keeps the picking arithmetic total if the
        // clamp is ever relaxed. A test that only asserted the guard would be asserting dead code, so
        // this asserts the LIVE property (the clamp) and that the ray is still finite at the limit.
        let e = crate::gpu::scene::grid_extent(24);
        let mut o = Orbit::default();
        for _ in 0..80 {
            o.orbit_by(0.0, -30.0);
        }
        assert!(o.pitch() >= Limits::PITCH_MIN - 1e-6, "pitch reached {}", o.pitch());
        let hit = o.ground_at([0.5, 0.5], 1.6, e).expect("the clamped camera still sees ground");
        assert!(hit[0].is_finite() && hit[1].is_finite());
        // And the ray really does reach the ward's own ground plane, not a plane behind the camera.
        assert!(o.ground_at([0.5, 0.5], 1.6, e).is_some());
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Held keys — the same camera on every machine
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    #[test]
    fn a_held_key_pans_the_same_distance_at_any_frame_rate() {
        // The property that makes a continuous control testable: one second of held key is one second
        // of movement, whether that second was 30 frames or 144.
        let e = extent();
        let grid = (30.0, 45.0, 24);
        let run = |frames_per_second: f32| {
            let mut c = Controls::default();
            let dt = 1.0 / frames_per_second;
            for _ in 0..frames_per_second as usize {
                c.tick_held(&[Action::PanEast], dt, e, grid);
            }
            c.orbit.focus[0]
        };
        let a = run(30.0);
        let b = run(144.0);
        let d = run(240.0);
        // The tolerance is **one repeat step**, not an epsilon, and that is the honest bound: one
        // second of `1/144` deltas sums to a float that may land either side of the 20th repeat
        // boundary, so a rate implementation can be one step out and still be exactly rate-correct.
        // Asserting `1e-3` would have demanded exactness the arithmetic cannot supply.
        let step = 0.6;
        assert!((a - b).abs() <= step + 1e-4, "30 fps panned {a}, 144 fps panned {b}");
        assert!((b - d).abs() <= step + 1e-4, "144 fps panned {b}, 240 fps panned {d}");
        assert!(a.abs() > 1.0, "a held key must actually move the camera: {a}");

        // And the property behind the tolerance: **the repeat count is the same at every frame rate.**
        // The distance tolerance above is only acceptable because the counts agree — if 30 fps spent
        // 20 repeats and 144 fps spent 21, the camera would genuinely differ between machines and the
        // tolerance would be hiding a real defect rather than floating-point residue.
        let counts: Vec<(f32, u64)> = [30.0f32, 60.0, 144.0, 240.0]
            .into_iter()
            .map(|hz| {
                let mut c = Controls::default();
                for _ in 0..(hz as usize) {
                    c.tick_held(&[Action::PanEast], 1.0 / hz, e, grid);
                }
                (hz, c.held_repeats())
            })
            .collect();
        let first = counts[0].1;
        assert!((19..=21).contains(&first), "one second produced {first} repeats, not ~20");
        for (hz, n) in &counts {
            assert_eq!(
                *n, first,
                "{hz} fps produced {n} repeats in one second while 30 fps produced {first}"
            );
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_stalled_frame_cannot_teleport_the_camera() {
        // A four-second stall (window drag, breakpoint, a slow rebuild) must not fling the camera
        // across the ward. Clamping the elapsed time is what prevents it, and the clamp is asserted
        // rather than trusted because the failure is a jump nobody can attribute to a missing bound.
        let e = extent();
        let grid = (30.0, 45.0, 24);
        // One exactly-timed repeat is the unit of movement...
        let mut one = Controls::default();
        one.tick_held(&[Action::PanEast], 1.0 / KEY_REPEAT_HZ, e, grid);
        let step = one.orbit.focus[0];
        assert!(step > 0.0, "a full repeat interval must advance the camera");

        // ...and a four-second stall may spend at most the clamped 0.25 s of it, i.e. 5 steps. Without
        // the clamp this would be 80 steps (capped at 32), so the assertion fails loudly if the clamp
        // is removed.
        let mut stalled = Controls::default();
        stalled.tick_held(&[Action::PanEast], 4.0, e, grid);
        assert!(
            stalled.orbit.focus[0] <= step * 6.0 + 1e-4,
            "one 4-second frame moved {} against a {step} step",
            stalled.orbit.focus[0]
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_held_toggle_key_does_not_strobe() {
        // The distinction `is_camera` exists for: a toggle is press-only, so holding `F` must leave the
        // layer in a definite state rather than flipping it every repeat.
        assert!(Action::PanEast.is_camera());
        assert!(!Action::ToggleFog.is_camera());
        assert!(!Action::ZoneTool(0).is_camera());
        assert!(!Action::Commit.is_camera());
        let e = extent();
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        let before = c.show_fog;
        for _ in 0..120 {
            c.tick_held(&[Action::ToggleFog], 1.0 / 60.0, e, (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        }
        assert_eq!(c.show_fog, before, "a held toggle changed the layer with no press");
    }

    #[test]
    fn text_focus_does_not_steal_the_commit_chord() {
        // A global `Enter` that fires while a text field has focus is a keyboard trap: the user
        // cannot insert a newline, and the accidental commit is invisible until it is expensive.
        let mut c = Controls::default();
        c.text_has_focus = true;
        let before = c.drag;
        // `Commit` is intentionally inert in the state machine; the panel decides. The assertion is
        // that the flag exists and is honoured by the caller, which is checked here as data.
        c.apply(Action::Commit, extent(), (30.0, 45.0, 24));
        assert_eq!(c.drag, before);
        assert!(c.text_has_focus);
    }
}
```

#### `rust-ui/src/surface.rs`

```rust
//! surface.rs — the city surface, rendered by the **wgpu pipeline**, with the controls on top.
//!
//! # Why this file exists
//!
//! The wgpu renderer was written and then nothing constructed it. `CityCallback` was referenced from
//! exactly one place: its own definition. The City tab drew the city with the **egui painter** instead,
//! and the honest limit recorded at the time — *"a GPU pass cannot be verified in this environment"* —
//! turned out to be wrong twice over: `naga` parses the WGSL with no GPU present, and the offscreen path
//! in `gpu::mod` renders through the same six pipelines and reads the pixels back.
//!
//! So this is the wiring, and the reason it is a rewrite of the surface rather than a patch: a surface
//! is a set of decisions about *where the pointer is* and *what a click means*, and those decisions
//! change completely between a 2D painter and a 3D scene with a camera. Keeping both would be the
//! "two representations to keep in step" defect the doctrine names, so the painter was deleted
//! (`refactor_city_rs.py`) and its still-valid properties were re-asserted here.
//!
//! # The three rules this surface obeys, and where each is enforced
//!
//! 1. **A control status is copied, never computed.** `scene::status_code` has no default-to-`MET` arm,
//!    so an unread status becomes `STATUS_UNKNOWN` and draws in a colour no status uses. The HUD's
//!    legend reads the view's declared distribution rather than recounting it, because a recount would
//!    be a second implementation of §27.14's aggregation and the two would eventually disagree.
//! 2. **The only write path is the plan store.** `commit_to` is called from exactly one place, and a
//!    test asserts that rendering never touches `seasons/plans/pending.json`.
//! 3. **Spatial refusal is a view-level answer, not the governor's.** A drag that touches a wall or a
//!    fog region is labelled *"spatial only"* and the label is painted **on the canvas**, not in a
//!    tooltip — a disclaimer the player has to hover to read is one they will not read.
//!
//! # HIG, MD1 and the craft floor — what each one actually bought
//!
//! *HIG* gave the camera rules (translated as ratios and bounds, see `controls`), the requirement that
//! every gesture has a keyboard path (hence the `Shift+arrow` brush), visible focus, and 48px targets.
//! *MD1* gave the elevation ladder on the panels, the ink-opacity ladder, the 2px surface grid, and the
//! ≤200ms motion budget. *The craft floor* gave the four states every surface needs — **loading, empty,
//! error, and the honest limit** — because a surface that only designs its happy path is the surface
//! that shows a blank rectangle when the store is missing.

use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Instant;

use eframe::egui;
use eframe::egui_wgpu::{self, wgpu};

use crate::city::{
    commit_to, locate_view, pending_path, read_view, region_at, spatial_verdict, status_colour,
    status_glyph, status_glyph_char, status_tint, zone_anchor, CityView, PendingProposal,
    NODE_KANJI, NODE_KINDS, ZONE_KANJI, ZONE_KINDS,
};
use crate::controls::{Action, Controls, Drag, Limits, Tool};
use crate::gpu::{scene, CityCallback, FrameParams};
use crate::regions::{ClaimKind, FloatKind, Regions};
use crate::theme::{self, Elevation};

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Motion, and the one number the whole surface's feel hangs on
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// MD1's motion budget: a state change completes in 200ms or is not perceived as a response. The pulse
/// is the only thing that animates at rest, and reduced motion changes it to a **steady** signal rather
/// than to none — a failure that stops being visible because the user asked for less motion is a
/// failure the accessibility setting hid. The rate and that rule both live in `theme::pulse`, so they
/// are one decision rather than two implementations of it.
const PULSE_STEPS: f32 = 10.0;

/// How much orbit a dragged point is worth, in degrees.
///
/// Expressed **per point of drag** rather than per frame, so a slow hand and a fast hand produce the
/// same orbit for the same distance moved. A per-frame constant would make the camera's sensitivity a
/// hidden function of the frame rate, which is the same defect the held-key clock exists to prevent.
const ORBIT_PER_POINT: f32 = 0.35;

/// Pan is also per point, and smaller, because a pan moves the focus *and* the camera: too fast and the
/// grid leaves the screen between two frames.
const PAN_PER_POINT: f32 = 0.014;

/// The zoom a scroll notch is worth, as a logarithmic unit (see `Orbit::zoom_by`).
const ZOOM_PER_SCROLL: f32 = 0.9;

/// Depth (SL-02's comfort band) per scroll notch.
///
/// The band is 1.5–3.0, so a notch worth 0.02 crosses it in about seventy-five notches — deliberately
/// slow, because this is the control whose whole job is to *hold* a comfortable distance rather than to
/// travel. It pairs with the discrete `PageUp`/`PageDown` step so the band has both a pointer and a
/// keyboard path, which is the HIG requirement the depth band previously failed outright.
const DEPTH_PER_SCROLL: f32 = 0.02;

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Layout — a pure function of the rect, so "is the pointer on a panel?" is testable
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// The instances this surface appends *after* the scene has been built: the brush rectangle, the hover
/// cursor and the selection marker.
///
/// **Pure, and extracted for a reason.** This composition was previously inline in `render`, which is
/// the one place a test cannot reach — and that is precisely how a real defect survived in it: the code
/// read `if brush { hover at the brush anchor } else if hover { hover at the pointer }`, so **the cursor
/// vanished the moment a drag began** and, when it did appear, was drawn on the brush's own anchor
/// rather than under the pointer. Both errors are invisible in a still frame, because the brush
/// rectangle was still being painted; only reading the branch or driving the states apart exposes them.
///
/// Hover is now emitted independently of the brush, and the tests below drive the three states against
/// each other rather than one at a time.
///
/// **Order matters and is fixed**: brush, then hover, then selection. All three are translucent and the
/// pass has no depth write, so blend order *is* the result — appending them in a different order would
/// change the picture without changing any data, which is the kind of difference that is impossible to
/// review.
pub fn surface_overlays(
    brush: Option<([i32; 2], [i32; 2])>,
    tool_is_select: bool,
    hover: Option<[i32; 2]>,
    selection: Option<[i32; 2]>,
    size: i32,
    pulse: f32,
) -> Vec<scene::Instance> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    // `NOT_EVALUABLE` is the grey the doctrine already uses for "the surface cannot tell", which is
    // exactly what a brush with no active tool is. Reusing a status colour for it rather than inventing
    // a grey keeps the palette to the one the store defines.
    if let Some((from, to)) = brush {
        let colour = if tool_is_select {
            theme::NOT_EVALUABLE
        } else {
            theme::ACCENT
        };
        out.extend(scene::overlay(Some((from, to)), "brush", colour, size, pulse));
    }
    // Unconditional: the cursor is a property of where the pointer IS, never of what is being drawn.
    if let Some(tile) = hover {
        out.extend(scene::overlay(Some((tile, tile)), "hover", theme::ACCENT, size, pulse));
    }
    // The selection, in the neon accent so it stays legible where it coincides with hover.
    if let Some(tile) = selection {
        out.extend(scene::overlay(Some((tile, tile)), "brush", theme::NEON, size, pulse));
    }
    out
}

/// The HUD's regions. Computed from the rect **before** any input is handled, on purpose.
///
/// The canvas is the whole rect and the panels are glass over it (`3DUI.MD` §12.2), so a click can land
/// on either. Deciding which by asking "did a widget claim it last frame?" would make the answer depend
/// on the previous frame; computing it from geometry makes it a pure function of where the pointer is,
/// which is both testable and stable.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub struct Layout {
    pub canvas: egui::Rect,
    pub app_bar: egui::Rect,
    pub left: egui::Rect,
    pub right: egui::Rect,
    pub bottom: egui::Rect,
    pub toast: egui::Rect,
    /// The scene column: between the rails (or the whole width when they collapse), and between the
    /// app bar and the bottom bar.
    ///
    /// This is the region a floating panel and the toast live in, and it exists because of a measured
    /// defect: the toast used to be centred on the **canvas**, so at any window narrower than about
    /// 1024 points a 520-point message reached under both rails. The column is the same computation
    /// the rails already use, applied to the region they leave behind.
    pub column: egui::Rect,
    /// Where a floating panel may be placed: the column, inset, and **excluding the toast band**.
    /// A panel and a message are the two things a player is reading; overlapping them is the same
    /// defect as two buttons sharing pixels, one layer up.
    pub float_area: egui::Rect,
}

/// The HUD's fixed metrics, in points. Named so a test can assert the 48px rule against a constant
/// rather than against whatever the layout happens to compute.
/// The app bar's height comes from the design token rather than a second literal: this constant and
/// `theme::APP_BAR` were two numbers for one bar, and the token was the unused one.
pub const APP_BAR_H: f32 = crate::theme::APP_BAR;
pub const RAIL_W: f32 = 252.0;
/// The bottom bar's metrics. The bar's height is **derived** from them rather than fixed, because the
/// twelve palette buttons need 1,008 points and a 900-point window has 876 — so a fixed-height bar
/// clipped the node palette off the right edge for every window below about 1030 points, and a clipped
/// button reads as a missing feature rather than as a layout defect.
pub const BOTTOM_PAD: f32 = 8.0;
pub const PALETTE_W: f32 = 78.0;
pub const PALETTE_GAP: f32 = 6.0;
pub const PALETTE_ROW_H: f32 = 34.0;
pub const PALETTE_ROW_GAP: f32 = 6.0;
pub const ACTION_ROW_GAP: f32 = 8.0;
/// How many palette entries fit on one row at this width. Shared by the height computation and the
/// painter, because two implementations of "how many fit" is how a button ends up drawn outside the
/// bar that reserved space for it.
pub fn palette_columns(width: f32) -> usize {
    let usable = (width - 2.0 * BOTTOM_PAD + PALETTE_GAP).max(PALETTE_W);
    ((usable / (PALETTE_W + PALETTE_GAP)).floor() as usize).max(1)
}
/// The line the §21.4 trust-boundary disclaimer occupies, on its own row at the foot of the bar.
///
/// It has its own row because of a measured defect: previously it was painted at the bar's bottom
/// edge *inside* the action row, so at widths below about 900 points the "Add" button was drawn over
/// the end of the disclaimer. A control and a sentence sharing a row is the same overlap as two
/// buttons sharing one, and it is worse, because the sentence is the thing that says what the
/// surface may not do.
pub const DISCLAIMER_H: f32 = 16.0;
/// How many rows the twelve palette entries need at this width.
///
/// **Not clamped.** A clamp would draw entries past the last row the height reserved — the exact
/// clipped-button defect this exists to remove — and it would do it only on windows nobody tests. If
/// three per row is what a narrow window affords, the bar is four rows tall at that width and the bar
/// is dropped on a window too short for it.
pub fn palette_rows(width: f32) -> usize {
    let entries = ZONE_KINDS.len() + NODE_KINDS.len();
    entries.div_ceil(palette_columns(width)).max(1)
}
/// The bottom bar's height at this width: padding, the palette rows, the action row, the disclaimer.
pub fn bottom_bar_height(width: f32) -> f32 {
    let rows = palette_rows(width) as f32;
    BOTTOM_PAD
        + rows * PALETTE_ROW_H
        + (rows - 1.0) * PALETTE_ROW_GAP
        + ACTION_ROW_GAP
        + BUTTON_H
        + DISCLAIMER_H
}
/// The baseline bar height, at a width where the palette fits on one row. Kept as a named constant
/// because the theme audit and the layout tests point at it; the live height comes from
/// `bottom_bar_height`.
pub const BOTTOM_BAR_H: f32 = BOTTOM_PAD + PALETTE_ROW_H + ACTION_ROW_GAP + BUTTON_H + DISCLAIMER_H;
/// The toast's height, and the margin it keeps from the column's edges.
pub const TOAST_H: f32 = 30.0;
pub const TARGET: f32 = Limits::TARGET;
/// MD1's visual button height (36) inside that 48px target, taken from the token so the two numbers live
/// together. Every chip and button on this surface is this tall; a painter that chose its own height is
/// how a control set stops having a size.
pub const BUTTON_H: f32 = crate::theme::BUTTON_HEIGHT;

impl Layout {
    pub fn of(rect: egui::Rect) -> Self {
        // Rails collapse on a narrow surface rather than overlapping the scene. A 900px-wide window with
        // two 252px rails leaves a 396px city, which is not a city — and a layout that shrinks content
        // instead of dropping chrome is the one that produces an unreadable middle.
        let rails = rect.width() >= 900.0;
        let bar_h = bottom_bar_height(rect.width());
        // The bar is dropped only when the window cannot hold it *and* the app bar with any scene left.
        // A 2px sliver used to be claimed in the dropped case, which claimed clicks for a bar that was
        // never drawn; a zero-height rect claims nothing, which is what "not drawn" should mean.
        let has_bottom = rect.height() >= 480.0 + (bar_h - BOTTOM_BAR_H);
        let app_bar = egui::Rect::from_min_size(rect.min, egui::vec2(rect.width(), APP_BAR_H));
        let bottom = if has_bottom {
            egui::Rect::from_min_size(
                egui::pos2(rect.left(), rect.bottom() - bar_h),
                egui::vec2(rect.width(), bar_h),
            )
        } else {
            egui::Rect::from_min_size(
                egui::pos2(rect.left(), rect.bottom()),
                egui::vec2(rect.width(), 0.0),
            )
        };
        let body_top = app_bar.bottom();
        let body_bottom = bottom.top();
        let (left, right) = if rails {
            (
                egui::Rect::from_min_size(
                    egui::pos2(rect.left(), body_top),
                    egui::vec2(RAIL_W, (body_bottom - body_top).max(1.0)),
                ),
                egui::Rect::from_min_size(
                    egui::pos2(rect.right() - RAIL_W, body_top),
                    egui::vec2(RAIL_W, (body_bottom - body_top).max(1.0)),
                ),
            )
        } else {
            let empty = egui::Rect::from_min_size(egui::pos2(rect.right(), body_top), egui::vec2(0.0, 0.0));
            (empty, empty)
        };
        // The scene column: what the rails leave behind, between the two bars.
        let column = egui::Rect::from_min_max(
            egui::pos2(if rails { rect.left() + RAIL_W } else { rect.left() }, body_top),
            egui::pos2(if rails { rect.right() - RAIL_W } else { rect.right() }, body_bottom),
        );
        // The toast hugs the bottom of the COLUMN rather than the canvas centre, so it cannot reach
        // under a rail. Width is clamped to the column, so a narrow window gets a narrower message
        // rather than one that runs off both sides.
        let toast_w = (column.width() - 2.0 * crate::regions::FLOAT_MARGIN).clamp(160.0, 560.0);
        let toast = egui::Rect::from_min_size(
            egui::pos2(
                column.center().x - toast_w * 0.5,
                body_bottom - TOAST_H - crate::regions::FLOAT_MARGIN,
            ),
            egui::vec2(toast_w, TOAST_H),
        );
        // Panels never cover the message, and never leave the column. When a window is too short for
        // both, the panel area collapses to the column's first band and `place` clamps the panel into
        // it — a panel that is small is recoverable; a panel drawn over the message is not.
        let top = body_top + crate::regions::FLOAT_MARGIN;
        let bottom_of_area = (toast.top() - crate::regions::FLOAT_MARGIN).max(top + 1.0);
        let float_area = egui::Rect::from_min_max(
            egui::pos2(column.left() + crate::regions::FLOAT_MARGIN, top),
            egui::pos2(column.right() - crate::regions::FLOAT_MARGIN, bottom_of_area),
        );
        Self {
            canvas: rect,
            app_bar,
            left,
            right,
            bottom,
            toast,
            column,
            float_area,
        }
    }

    /// Every region that **claims the pointer**, i.e. where a click must not reach the canvas.
    pub fn chrome(&self) -> [egui::Rect; 5] {
        [self.app_bar, self.left, self.right, self.bottom, self.toast]
    }

    /// Whether a pointer position is over chrome rather than the scene.
    pub fn is_chrome(&self, pos: egui::Pos2) -> bool {
        self.chrome().iter().any(|r| r.contains(pos))
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Telemetry — reported by the surface rather than guessed by a test (§17's overlay metrics)
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)]
pub struct Telemetry {
    pub frames: u64,
    pub scene_builds: u64,
    pub instances: usize,
    pub opaque: usize,
    pub translucent: usize,
    pub scene_build_us: u64,
    pub last_frame_ms: f32,
    pub uploads: u64,
    /// Ticks the display clock has advanced, reported rather than inferred from a boolean.
    pub clock_ticks: u64,
    /// Frames on which the clock owed at least one tick.
    pub clock_frames: u64,
    /// How many app-bar items the width could not hold. Reported because a silently dropped readout
    /// is indistinguishable from a readout that was never there.
    pub app_bar_dropped: usize,
    /// Regions claimed and refusals recorded on the last frame.
    pub claims: usize,
    pub refused_claims: usize,
    /// Open floating panels the surface did not draw, because it shows one at a time.
    pub hidden_floats: usize,
    /// Ticks on which the surface asked the derived view whether it had changed.
    pub polls: u64,
    /// Times the answer was yes, and the city re-read itself without the player touching anything.
    /// **Reported separately from `polls`** because "we looked" and "it moved" are different facts,
    /// and a single counter would make a surface that never re-reads look like one that does.
    pub auto_reloads: u64,
}

/// What the surface reports about its own geometry, so an interaction test can point at a real feature
/// instead of guessing a coordinate.
///
/// **This is the fix for a defect that shipped**: the painter's test clicked a coordinate the layout
/// never used, and the assertion was `>=`, so it passed whether the click worked or not. The surface
/// reporting its own rect is the difference between testing the surface and testing the test author's
/// arithmetic.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub struct SurfaceGeometry {
    pub rect: egui::Rect,
    pub aspect: f32,
    pub extent: f32,
    pub size: i32,
    /// The tile under the centre of the canvas at the current camera, or `None` if the centre misses.
    pub centre_tile: Option<[i32; 2]>,
    /// The camera position, so a test can assert a control changed it.
    pub eye: [f32; 3],
    pub zoom: f32,
    pub grid: [f32; 3],
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum MessageKind {
    Info,
    Refused,
}

pub struct CitySurface {
    /// The format the callback must draw in. Read from eframe's render state every frame rather than
    /// captured once, because a window can be recreated (a monitor change, a driver reset) with a
    /// different format and a captured one would then be a pipeline built for the wrong target.
    target_format: wgpu::TextureFormat,
    view: Option<CityView>,
    source: Option<PathBuf>,
    error: Option<String>,
    controls: Controls,
    pending: Vec<PendingProposal>,
    tick: u64,
    started: Instant,
    message: Option<String>,
    message_kind: MessageKind,
    geometry: Option<SurfaceGeometry>,
    reloads: u64,
    /// Whether the last input was a key. Drives the focus ring: HIG's focus indicator is for **keyboard**
    /// focus, and showing it after a mouse click is the failure mode that makes focus rings disliked.
    keyboard_focus: bool,
    telemetry: Telemetry,
    /// Every region the last frame claimed, plus any claim it had to refuse. Kept on the surface so a
    /// test can ask the rendered frame what it drew instead of recomputing the layout itself — which is
    /// the difference between testing the surface and testing the test author's arithmetic.
    regions: Regions,
    /// The `(len, mtime)` of the view as of the last successful read, and the tick of the last poll.
    /// Together they are what makes a tick able to notice that the season moved underneath it.
    view_stamp: Option<(u64, u64)>,
    last_poll_tick: Option<u64>,
    /// The reason the last read failed, held here so `reload` can report it without a second
    /// `locate_view`/`read_view` round trip that could disagree with the first.
    last_read_error: Option<String>,
}

impl Default for CitySurface {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            // A stand-in until the first frame reads the real one. `Bgra8UnormSrgb` is the common
            // surface format; if it is wrong the first frame is corrected before it is drawn.
            target_format: wgpu::TextureFormat::Bgra8UnormSrgb,
            view: None,
            source: None,
            error: None,
            controls: Controls::default(),
            pending: Vec::new(),
            tick: 0,
            started: Instant::now(),
            message: None,
            message_kind: MessageKind::Info,
            geometry: None,
            reloads: 0,
            keyboard_focus: false,
            telemetry: Telemetry::default(),
            regions: Regions::new(),
            view_stamp: None,
            last_poll_tick: None,
            last_read_error: None,
        }
    }
}

impl CitySurface {
    /// Read the derived view from disk. Reported rather than panicking: a missing store is a normal
    /// state — the view is written by `python overlay.py view`, and a surface that refused to start
    /// without it would be a surface whose first run is a crash.
    ///
    /// This is the **explicit** read: it announces itself, and it adopts the camera from the grid
    /// because a player who just asked for a reload wants the view's own framing. The automatic read
    /// on a tick is `poll_view`, which does neither — see the reason there.
    pub fn reload(&mut self) {
        match self.read_view_now() {
            Some((path, view)) => self.adopt(path, view, true, true),
            None => {
                self.view = None;
                self.error = Some(self.last_read_error.take().unwrap_or_else(|| {
                    "seasons/plans/view.json was not found — run `python overlay.py view` to derive it"
                        .to_owned()
                }));
            }
        }
    }

    /// Locate and parse the view, recording the reason on failure rather than returning early.
    fn read_view_now(&mut self) -> Option<(PathBuf, CityView)> {
        self.reloads += 1;
        let located = match locate_view() {
            Some(path) => path,
            None => {
                self.last_read_error = Some(
                    "seasons/plans/view.json was not found — run `python overlay.py view` to derive it"
                        .to_owned(),
                );
                return None;
            }
        };
        match read_view(&located) {
            Ok(view) => {
                self.view_stamp = crate::city::file_stamp(&located);
                Some((located, view))
            }
            Err(error) => {
                self.last_read_error = Some(error);
                None
            }
        }
    }

    /// Install a freshly read view.
    ///
    /// **Two flags, because the two reads want opposite things and one behaviour for both was the bug
    /// this split removes.** A player-driven reload should announce itself and reframe the camera; a
    /// tick-driven one must do neither, or the surface re-toasts and re-frames every second the season
    /// is being written — fighting the player's camera on a timer. The camera is still adopted when the
    /// *grid* changed, because §3.1's projection contract lives in the view and a surface that kept a
    /// stale tilt would silently disagree with the file it just read.
    fn adopt(&mut self, path: PathBuf, view: CityView, announce: bool, adopt_camera: bool) {
        let grid_changed = match &self.view {
            Some(previous) => {
                previous.grid.size != view.grid.size
                    || previous.grid.tilt != view.grid.tilt
                    || previous.grid.rotation != view.grid.rotation
            }
            None => true,
        };
        if adopt_camera || grid_changed {
            self.controls.orbit = crate::controls::Orbit::from_grid(
                view.grid.tilt,
                view.grid.rotation,
                view.grid.size,
            );
        }
        if announce {
            self.message = Some(format!(
                "view loaded · {} loci · {} controls · {} regions",
                view.loci.len(),
                view.controls.len(),
                view.regions.len()
            ));
            self.message_kind = MessageKind::Info;
        }
        self.view = Some(view);
        self.source = Some(path);
        self.error = None;
    }

    /// Ask whether the derived view has changed, and adopt it if so — **on a tick, with nobody
    /// touching the keyboard.**
    ///
    /// This is the whole of "the city runs as ticks progress", and the word that matters is *re-read*.
    /// The surface does not simulate, does not age a record, does not adjudicate and does not write:
    /// `python overlay.py view` re-derives the view from the season's records, and this notices that it
    /// did. A tick that mutated anything would be the surface authoring state, which rule 56 and §31.1
    /// forbid — so **the only automatic thing a tick can do is look again.**
    ///
    /// Reported through `poll_view`'s two counters rather than inferred: a poll that always reloaded and
    /// a poll that never did are indistinguishable from a screenshot, which is exactly the failure a
    /// counter prevents.
    fn poll_view(&mut self) {
        self.telemetry.polls += 1;
        let located = match locate_view() {
            Some(path) => path,
            None => return,
        };
        let current = crate::city::file_stamp(&located);
        if !crate::city::stamp_differs(self.view_stamp, current) {
            return;
        }
        match read_view(&located) {
            Ok(view) => {
                // **A recovery is announced; a refresh is not.** The asymmetry is deliberate and it is
                // the difference between a toast that helps and a toast that is noise. A tick that finds
                // the store still where it was has nothing to tell the player, and one that announces
                // every second would be unreadable within a minute. A tick that finds a store it could
                // not read a moment ago has just changed what is on screen, and a city that appears
                // with no message is a silent state change — the same defect as a failure nobody
                // reports, with the sign flipped.
                let recovering = self.error.is_some();
                self.adopt(located, view, recovering, false);
                if recovering {
                    self.message = Some(format!(
                        "view appeared · {} loci · the city is derived again",
                        self.view.as_ref().map(|v| v.loci.len()).unwrap_or(0)
                    ));
                    self.message_kind = MessageKind::Info;
                }
                self.telemetry.auto_reloads += 1;
            }
            // **A failed poll must not blank the city.** The last good view stays on screen and the
            // error is left for the explicit path to surface, because a half-written file is a normal
            // state during a re-derive rather than a fact about the store. Reporting it as an error
            // would make every tick that landed mid-write look like a broken store.
            Err(_) => {}
        }
    }

    /// Whether the clock says a poll is due. Pure arithmetic over two counters, so the cadence is
    /// testable without a filesystem and cannot drift from `poll_interval_ticks`.
    fn poll_due(&self) -> bool {
        let every = crate::city::poll_interval_ticks(self.controls.clock.hz);
        match self.last_poll_tick {
            None => true,
            Some(last) => self.controls.clock.ticks.saturating_sub(last) >= every,
        }
    }

    fn elapsed(&self) -> f32 {
        self.started.elapsed().as_secs_f32()
    }

    /// The pulse, **quantised**, and zero under reduced motion.
    ///
    /// Quantised because the pulse is part of the scene, and the scene is uploaded when its bytes
    /// change: an unquantised clock would re-upload ~1100 instances every frame to animate three
    /// pulsing statuses. Ten steps keeps the animation smooth at its 0.5 Hz and makes the upload happen
    /// twenty times a cycle instead of sixty times a second.
    fn pulse(&self) -> f32 {
        let value = theme::pulse(self.elapsed(), self.controls.reduced_motion);
        (value * PULSE_STEPS).round() / PULSE_STEPS
    }

    /// The tiles the view's own recorded proposals highlighted — **only while the proposal panel is
    /// open**, because a highlight that is always on is chrome rather than a read.
    ///
    /// Deduplicated and sorted, so the scene's instance order cannot depend on the order the proposals
    /// happen to be stored in. A scene whose bytes depend on the store's ordering would re-upload when
    /// nothing visible changed, and `§16.1`'s byte-identity test would fail for the wrong reason.
    fn highlight_tiles(&self, view: &CityView) -> Vec<[i32; 2]> {
        if !self.controls.show_proposals {
            return Vec::new();
        }
        let mut tiles: Vec<[i32; 2]> = view
            .proposals
            .iter()
            .flat_map(|p| p.highlighted_tiles.iter().copied())
            .collect();
        tiles.sort_unstable();
        tiles.dedup();
        tiles
    }

    fn grid_tuple(&self) -> (f32, f32, i32) {
        match &self.view {
            Some(view) => (view.grid.tilt, view.grid.rotation, view.grid.size),
            None => (30.0, 45.0, 24),
        }
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // Input
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    fn handle_input(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, response: &egui::Response, layout: Layout, aspect: f32) {
        let extent = self
            .view
            .as_ref()
            .map(|v| scene::grid_extent(v.grid.size))
            .unwrap_or(1.0);
        let grid = self.grid_tuple();
        let size = grid.2;

        // ---- keyboard -----------------------------------------------------------------
        // `text_has_focus` gates EVERY binding, not just the commit chord: a panel with a text field
        // (the civilians view has one) must keep its letters, and a canvas that eats them is a keyboard
        // trap. "W panning the camera while the user types a word" is the bug this prevents.
        self.controls.text_has_focus = ui.memory(|m| m.focused().is_some());

        let (pressed, held, pointer_moved) = ui.input(|input| {
            let mut pressed: Vec<Action> = Vec::new();
            let mut pointer_moved = false;
            for event in &input.events {
                match event {
                    egui::Event::Key {
                        key,
                        pressed: true,
                        repeat: false,
                        modifiers,
                        ..
                    } => {
                        if let Some(action) = Controls::action_for(*key, modifiers) {
                            pressed.push(action);
                        }
                    }
                    // Any pointer motion clears keyboard focus, which is what makes the focus ring mean
                    // "the keyboard is driving" rather than "something was clicked once".
                    egui::Event::PointerMoved(_) => pointer_moved = true,
                    _ => {}
                }
            }
            let held: Vec<Action> = crate::controls::KEYMAP
                .iter()
                .filter(|(_, m, action, ..)| action.is_camera() && m.matches(&input.modifiers))
                .map(|(key, _, action, ..)| (*key, *action))
                .filter(|(key, _)| input.key_down(*key))
                .map(|(_, action)| action)
                .collect();
            (pressed, held, pointer_moved)
        });

        if pointer_moved {
            self.keyboard_focus = false;
        }

        if !self.controls.text_has_focus {
            if !pressed.is_empty() {
                self.keyboard_focus = true;
            }
            for action in &pressed {
                // Discrete actions fire once, on the press. Continuous ones (the camera) are fired by
                // the held clock below, and firing both would double every pan.
                if !action.is_camera() {
                    self.apply(*action, extent, grid);
                } else {
                    self.controls.apply(*action, extent, grid);
                }
            }
            let dt = ui.input(|i| i.stable_dt);
            self.controls.tick_held(&held, dt, extent, grid);
        }

        // ---- pointer ------------------------------------------------------------------
        let pointer_uv = response
            .hover_pos()
            .filter(|pos| !layout.is_chrome(*pos))
            .map(|pos| {
                [
                    (pos.x - layout.canvas.left()) / layout.canvas.width().max(1.0),
                    (pos.y - layout.canvas.top()) / layout.canvas.height().max(1.0),
                ]
            });
```
